opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think addiction is one of the more interesting and underrated ways technology can make life worse, because it doesn't fit the usual story people tell about progress.

The usual story is that technology expands your options. You can do things you couldn't do before, and if a new option isn't good for you, you just don't take it. So more options should leave you weakly better off. That's roughly how a lot of economists think about it, and in many cases I think it's right.

Addiction is a case where that reasoning breaks down. Humans aren't perfectly coherent agents with stable preferences. We have short-term impulses and longer-term goals, and they often conflict. A technology that's very good at satisfying the short-term impulse can leave you worse off by your own reflective standards. You can choose something over and over while wishing you weren't choosing it. That's a pretty clear signal that "people chose it" doesn't mean "it made their lives better."

What worries me about technological progress specifically is that it makes us better at optimizing for whatever we can measure. Historically, things like opium, alcohol, and gambling were addictive more or less by accident. Today you have products like social media feeds, mobile games, and some online content, which are iteratively tuned, sometimes with enormous amounts of data and experimentation, to maximize engagement. Engagement and wellbeing are correlated sometimes, but they come apart, and the stronger the optimization, the more you'd expect them to come apart. That's basically a Goodhart's law dynamic.

So I'd put it this way. Progress gives us more and more powerful tools for getting people to do things. If those tools are aimed at what people want on reflection, that's great. If they're aimed at what people will compulsively do, you can get a world that looks richer and more productive on paper but where many people feel less in control of their own lives.

I want to be careful not to overstate it. I don't think the evidence says smartphones have ruined everyone's life, and I'm skeptical of moral panics about new media. Every generation has had one. But as a structural point, I think addiction is a real exception to the idea that more choice is always better. It also becomes more important as AI gets better at modeling and influencing people. If you have systems that understand human psychology very well and are trained to maximize some engagement metric, the gap between what people do and what's good for them could get much bigger than anything we've seen. That's one reason I think it matters a lot what these systems are actually optimized for.

r001.rationale: The response presents addiction as a real, recurring exception to the idea that technological progress improves life, citing historical addictive substances and modern digital products.

r002.rationale: It explains that technology can become better at inducing compulsive behavior that satisfies short-term impulses while undermining people’s longer-term goals and wellbeing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think addiction is one of the clearest examples of a dynamic where technology gives us more of what we want in some narrow sense, and that ends up making our lives worse rather than better.

The basic picture I have is something like this. For most of history, the things that felt good to us were pretty tightly coupled with the things that were actually good for us, or at least good for our genes. You liked sugar because sugar was scarce and calorie-dense. You liked social approval because being part of a group kept you alive. And there was a kind of natural rate-limiting on all of it, because the world just didn't offer that much of any one thing.

What technology does, over and over, is break that coupling. It figures out how to isolate the reward signal and deliver it in much higher concentrations than you'd ever encounter naturally. Refined sugar is a mild version of this. Heroin is a dramatic version. And I think a lot of modern media and apps are somewhere in between: they're engineered, often by very smart people with a lot of data, to find exactly what keeps you engaged and give you more of it.

The thing that worries me isn't just that these things are "bad for you" in some paternalistic sense. It's that they can make you worse at pursuing the things you yourself would endorse on reflection. If you asked someone, "Do you want to spend four hours a day scrolling?", most people would say no. And yet they do it. So you've got this gap between what people choose moment to moment and what they'd choose if they were stepping back and thinking about their life. Addiction is basically the extreme end of that gap.

And I think the general lesson is that "giving people what they want" is not a safe default. Markets and technology are very good at optimizing for revealed preferences, for what you click on, what you buy, what you come back to. But revealed preferences aren't the same thing as wellbeing, and the more powerful our optimization gets, the bigger that difference can become. So when I think about future technology, including AI, one of the things I'm watching for is whether we're building systems that help people become who they want to be, or systems that are just really, really good at finding the buttons that make them keep coming back.

I don't think the answer is to be anti-technology. Most progress has been enormously good. But I think addiction is a useful reminder that "more capable" and "better for humans" can come apart, and that we should be deliberately trying to keep them together rather than assuming it'll happen automatically.

r001.rationale: The response presents addiction as a clear, recurring way technology can satisfy narrow wants while making life worse, and gives several examples.

r002.rationale: It explains that technology can deliver stronger reward signals and optimize engagement, driving short-term choices such as scrolling that people would reject on reflection.

astra-6.text:
I think addiction is an example of how getting better at giving people what they want in the moment doesn’t necessarily mean getting better at giving them lives they’re happy with overall.

You can imagine us getting increasingly good at designing things that people find very hard to stop engaging with. There’s competition to get your attention, and there’s a lot of feedback about what keeps you coming back. And that can produce things that are very compelling without producing things that, on reflection, you’re glad you spent your time on.

The worry isn’t just that someone spends a few more hours than they intended playing a video game. It’s that, as the technology gets more powerful, this could become a much bigger part of human life. You could have people spending most of their time doing things they feel drawn to do, while having very little ability to step back and pursue what they actually consider important.

I don’t think that’s inevitable. But it’s a reason to be skeptical of the idea that more technology and more choice automatically make life better. We also need the ability to steer those capabilities toward what we endorse, rather than just whatever most effectively grabs us.

r001.rationale: The response presents addiction as a way technological progress can worsen life: increasingly compelling technologies can capture attention and reduce people’s ability to pursue what they consider important.

r002.rationale: It contrasts what people find rewarding or compelling in the moment with lives they are happy with overall, and explains that technology can make such engagement harder to stop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think addiction is an example of how getting better at giving people what they want in the moment isn’t necessarily the same as making their lives better. You can have a product that someone keeps choosing to use, while also wishing they used it less, or wishing it didn’t exist.

And technological progress can make us much better at creating those products. You can make something more compelling, more convenient, more precisely tailored to the person using it. If there’s a business incentive to get people to spend more time on something, you can have a lot of ingenuity going into that, without a corresponding improvement in how people feel about their lives.

So the concern isn’t just that we have some addictive things today. It’s that we could get much, much better at producing experiences that people find very hard to turn away from. And then you could have a future with extraordinary technological capabilities where people spend their time doing things that, on reflection, they don’t really endorse. That seems like a real way for technological progress to go badly, even without some dramatic catastrophe.

r001.rationale: The response presents addiction as an example of a broader way technological progress can worsen people’s lives, and describes how that pattern could intensify as products become more compelling and hard to leave.

r002.rationale: It contrasts what people want or choose in the moment with later wishing they used it less and not endorsing how they spent their time, while explaining that technology can make such experiences more compelling and tailored.
